question: If AI starts to improve itself quickly, who should decide when it must slow down?
reflection: Progress is safest when the people building powerful tools agree, in the open, on where to stop and check.
one_line: AI labs are starting to talk openly about shared limits on progress, just as AI shows real signs of doing original science.

top_stories.title: OpenAI proposes shared speed limits for frontier AI
top_stories.what: OpenAI's chief scientist suggested that all leading labs agree on capability levels they will not pass until safety monitoring catches up, measured with a prediction score called perplexity, and OpenAI published its own numbers first.
top_stories.why: Who sets the limits, and whether self-reported numbers can be trusted, is a governance question that public bodies in the region will soon need a view on.

top_stories.title: A famous maths problem may have been solved with Claude
top_stories.what: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis, and maintainers of the Lean proof-checking system reportedly said they have strong confidence in the machine-checked proof.
top_stories.why: If confirmed, it shows AI can contribute original research, which raises the value of careful human checking and explanation in every field.

top_stories.title: AI is tested on careful scientific judgement
top_stories.what: Lawrence Livermore researchers built a test where AI agents run their own experiments with a possibly broken simulator, and report results with honest error ranges; only the strongest models handled it well.
top_stories.why: Honest uncertainty is exactly what decision makers need from AI, and how people read those ranges is a behavioural-science question.

top_stories.title: Drug discovery gets a new AI exam
top_stories.what: OpenAI released MedChemBench, where its best model read chemical structures almost perfectly but picked good drug candidates only about half the time, while big drugmakers say AI is already shortening early research.
top_stories.why: Health clients should see AI as strong at reading and summarising, but still weak at the judgement calls that need expert review.

top_stories.title: Anthropic's listing mostly rewards existing giants
top_stories.what: Filings show Amazon and Google hold very large stakes in Anthropic and also sell it computing power, while its shares slipped after a strong first day.
top_stories.why: The gains from AI are flowing to a few firms, so questions of fair sharing and worker voice will grow in policy debates.

saudi_lens.text: President Trump said US tech firms could face a large tax for building AI data centres abroad, with no detail yet. Saudi plans that rely on US cloud firms building locally should track this closely.
A new Stanford-founded lab, Noeri, argues for many small models tuned to a place or people. That vision suits Arabic-first models trained on local data.

idea.title: Does showing AI uncertainty change decisions?
idea.pitch: Run an experiment where officials see the same AI estimate with and without an error range, and measure trust, choices and over-reliance.
idea.first_step: Pick one real forecast a client uses and design two versions of how it is shown.

idea_kids.title: How sure are you?
idea_kids.pitch: A card game where children answer guessing questions, then bet tokens on how sure they are, learning that saying 'I am not sure' is a strength.
idea_kids.first_step: Write 30 guessing cards about Saudi geography, animals and everyday numbers.

terms.definition: A score of how well a model predicts the next word in text it has not seen. Lower means the model is less surprised and usually more capable.
When a system's stated certainty matches how often it is actually right.
Checking a proof or program with software that tests every logical step, so errors cannot slip through.
